cards.name: Arrange flowers together
cards.summary: Choose, trim and place flowers or leafy stems in a jar or vase together.
materials: A small bunch of flowers or leafy stems, checked as safe to handle
A jar, mug or vase that will not tip easily
Water in a jug
Scissors or pruners for the helper
An old towel or newspaper for the table
steps: Spread the towel on the table and lay the stems out side by side.
Fill the jar about halfway with water together.
Look at the stems together and ask which one they would like to start with.
Trim the end of that stem so it fits the jar. The helper can do the cutting.
Place the first stem in the jar, or hand it over so they can place it.
Take turns choosing and adding stems. There is no right shape.
Turn the jar around and look at it from each side together.
Agree on where the flowers should go, such as a windowsill or the table.
safety: Some common flowers and plants, such as lily of the valley, foxglove and daffodils, are toxic if eaten. Check every plant before use.
Lilies shed pollen that stains and can irritate skin; remove the pollen tips or choose other flowers.
Remove thorns and prickly leaves from roses and holly before handing stems over.
Keep scissors and pruners with the helper, and wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.
Supervise closely if petals or leaves might be put in the mouth.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two stems. A single flower in a jar is a finished arrangement. Put it somewhere it can be seen and enjoyed.

cards.name: Decorate a keepsake box
cards.summary: Cover a shoebox with paper or fabric, then choose a few small things to keep inside.
materials: An empty shoebox or small cardboard box with a lid
Wrapping paper, wallpaper scraps or light fabric, cut a little larger than each side of the box
A glue stick or double-sided tape
Scissors for the helper
A few small items chosen by the person, such as a ribbon, a shell or a copy of a photo
steps: Set the box on the table with the lid off, and lay out the paper, the glue and the small items.
Choose the paper or fabric together. Any choice is fine.
Lay the paper on one side of the box, and ask the helper to trim it to a little larger than that side.
Glue the back of the paper, press it onto the box, then fold the extra over the edges and smooth it flat.
Turn the box and repeat on each side, then cover the lid the same way.
Set the box aside for a few minutes so the glue holds.
Look through the small items together and choose a few to keep inside.
Place the chosen items in the box and put the lid on.
Agree on a place to keep the box, such as a shelf or the bedside table.
safety: Scissors are for the helper only, and keep the glue away from the mouth.
Use a glue stick or double-sided tape rather than spray glue.
Choose items too large to swallow, and leave out pins, buttons or anything sharp.
Use copies of photos or papers, and keep the originals somewhere safe.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one side. Put the box and its paper aside, and carry on another day, or simply enjoy a few of the items together.

cards.name: Decorate a plant pot
cards.summary: A plain pot decorated with paint, paper or twine, ready for a plant or herb to live in.
materials: A small terracotta or plastic plant pot
Non-toxic, water-based paint and a thick-handled brush
Garden twine or yarn (optional)
Paper napkins or magazine pictures with a glue stick (optional)
Newspaper to cover the table
A small plant, herb or bulb, and a little potting soil
steps: Cover the table and put the pot and materials within reach.
Offer two ways to decorate, such as paint or wrapped twine, and let them choose.
Paint the outside of the pot, or wrap twine around it while you hold the end in place.
Leave paint to dry for about an hour; twine is ready straight away.
Smell the plant or herb together and talk about where it might sit.
Spoon soil into the pot and set the plant in it, taking turns if that suits you both.
Water it lightly and put it on a windowsill or table where you can both see it.
safety: Use non-toxic, water-based paint, and wash it off skin with soap and water.
Wear gloves or wash hands after handling potting soil, and keep it away from mouths.
Choose plants that are safe to touch and not harmful if nibbled, such as basil, mint or parsley.
Check food cans for sharp rims before use, and tape over any rough edge.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop once the pot is painted. Let it dry and plant it another day, or use it as it is for pens, buttons or dried flowers.

cards.name: Draw a comic strip together
cards.summary: Take turns drawing three or four boxes of a comic strip about something ordinary, such as the cat or breakfast.
materials: Plain paper, one sheet for each strip
Pencils
Markers or crayons, washable if possible
A ruler, optional
A clipboard or tray to rest the paper on, optional
steps: Fold or draw lines to make three or four boxes on one sheet, in a row or a grid.
Choose something ordinary to draw about together, such as the cat, breakfast or the walk to the shop.
Say in one short line what happens in each box. Keep it simple, and let the other person change it if they like.
One person draws the first box while the other says what is in it. Stick figures and simple shapes are fine.
Swap, so the other person draws the next box.
Add a few words in a speech bubble if you like, written by whoever is holding the pencil.
Draw the last box together, with an ending that is funny or quiet, whichever you prefer.
Read the strip out loud, then put it where you can both see it. Stop here, or start a second strip.
safety: Use washable markers if you can, and keep ink off skin that is sensitive.
Keep pencils and markers away from the mouth if anyone may chew or taste things.
Stay close, so the pencil and the paper are always easy to reach.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one box. Keep what is drawn, or add the next box another day. A strip with only one box is still a finished picture.

cards.name: Draw a map of a favorite place
cards.summary: Draw a simple map together of a place they know well or like, and talk about it as it grows.
materials: A large sheet of plain paper
A thick marker, or pencils or crayons
A firm board or tray to rest on, if working in a chair or bed
steps: Sit side by side with the paper between you and the pens within reach.
Ask whether there is a place they would like to draw, such as a street, a garden, a kitchen or a beach.
Make the first mark together, such as a line for a road or a shape for a house. Any mark will do.
Ask what comes next, and draw it or hand them the pen. Any answer is the right one.
Add one thing at a time, and let them talk or stay quiet as they choose.
Do not correct what they draw or say. Do not ask for dates or names.
Stop when it feels finished, or when they have had enough, and agree where to put the map.
safety: A place can bring back strong feelings. Listen kindly and let them lead. Offer to put the pen down, or move on to something lighter.
Never use the map to test them. Do not correct details or ask for dates, names or what happened.
Keep the helper nearby and offer to draw. They do not need to be good at drawing, and neither do you.
If a memory seems to upset them, stop drawing, sit with them and offer a drink or a change of scene.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one line. Put the map somewhere safe and carry on another day, or simply talk about the place for a while, or about something else.

cards.name: Draw a slow line pattern
cards.summary: Trace a circle round a cup, split it into sections and fill each with slow, repeating lines.
materials: A sheet of plain paper
A cup or small bowl with a round rim, to trace round
A soft pencil or a thick marker
A second pen in another color, if wanted
steps: Set the paper in front of the person and choose a pencil or marker together.
Hold the cup steady on the paper while they trace round its rim to make a circle.
Draw three or four curved or straight lines across the circle to split it into sections.
Pick one section and fill it with a slow repeat, such as short lines all leaning one way.
Move to the next section and try a different repeat, such as small circles, dots or zigzags.
Go one section at a time, resting the pencil between sections if you like.
Stop when the circle is full or whenever they want to, then turn the page around and look at it together.
safety: Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons and keep them away from the mouth.
Put the caps back on markers when not in use, since they dry out and can stain skin.
Choose a pencil with a blunt, soft tip, and keep the tip pointing away from the face.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one section. Put the page aside and look at it later, or simply watch the lines being drawn without adding any.

cards.name: Draw repeating patterns
cards.summary: Fill boxes on a page with simple repeating lines, loops and dots.
materials: A sheet of plain paper, with a grid of large boxes drawn on it
A soft pencil, a thick marker or a crayon
A ruler, if the boxes need to be drawn
steps: Place the paper on the table, with the grid of boxes facing the person.
Choose a pencil or marker together, and offer a choice of color if they want one.
Make a short line or a dot in the first box, and invite them to copy it or add their own.
Fill the box with a simple repeat, such as lines going the same way or loops in a row.
Move to the next box and try a different repeat, such as dots, zigzags or circles.
Keep going one box at a time for as long as it feels pleasant.
Stop when the page is full or when they want to stop, then look at the pattern together.
safety: Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons, and keep them away from the mouth.
Put the caps back on markers when not in use, since they dry out and can stain skin.
If a ruler is used, choose one with a rounded edge, or none at all.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one box or a few lines. Put the page aside and look at it together later, or simply watch the marks being made without adding more.

cards.name: Draw to music
cards.summary: Listen to music together and let lines, shapes and colors follow the sound.
materials: Large sheets of plain paper
Crayons, colored pencils or washable markers
A phone, radio or music player
A short list of three or four pieces of music with different moods
Masking tape to hold the paper still
steps: Tape a sheet of paper to the table so it does not slide.
Lay out the crayons or markers and offer a choice of color.
Play the first piece of music at a comfortable volume.
Draw lines or shapes together that follow the music, fast or slow, big or small.
Swap colors whenever either of you likes.
Stop the music and look at the drawing together. Talk about it only if they want to.
Try a different piece of music on a new sheet, or stop there.
safety: Keep the volume comfortable and check hearing aids are in and switched on. Avoid sudden loud music.
Use washable, non-toxic markers or crayons. Marker on skin usually washes off with soap and water; avoid drawing on skin.
Keep pens and crayons away from the mouth if the person may chew or taste things.
Some music brings up strong feelings. If they seem upset, pause, offer comfort, and switch to something calm.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few marks or a single song. Keep listening together without drawing, or put the music on for a quiet moment instead.

cards.name: Draw with oil pastels on dark paper
cards.summary: Draw simple shapes, a sky or a flower in bright oil pastels on black or dark paper.
materials: Oil pastels in bright colors, a box of 12 or more
Black or dark blue construction paper
A clipboard or flat board to rest the paper on
Newspaper or an old cloth to cover the table
Paper towels or baby wipes for fingers
steps: Spread newspaper over the table and rest the dark paper on a clipboard or flat board.
Open the pastels and set out a few bright colors where they are easy to reach.
Ask which color they would like to start with. Any choice is fine.
Draw a shape or a line on the dark paper, pressing firmly so the color shows clearly.
Add one thing at a time: a sky of colored bands, a sun, a flower, or just lines.
Lay a second color over the first if they like. The colors will blend together.
Wipe fingers on a paper towel when the pastel gets onto them.
Stop when they put the pastel down, then look at the picture together and choose where to put it.
safety: Oil pastels are waxy and can stain skin, clothes and furniture, so cover the table and wipe fingers as you go.
Oil pastels are not food. Keep them away from the mouth if anyone may chew or taste things.
Pick up broken bits and crumbs from the floor so no one treads on them.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one mark. Put the pastels away, or leave the page out and add to it another day. One bold line is already a picture.

cards.name: Fold a paper boat
cards.summary: A classic folded paper boat made from a single sheet, which you can float together in a basin of water.
materials: A rectangular sheet of paper, such as printer paper or newspaper
A flat, clear table
A wide basin or tray of shallow water (optional)
A towel for drying hands
steps: Fold the sheet in half from top to bottom and run a thumbnail along the crease.
Fold the two top corners down to the middle to make a triangle.
Fold the bottom strip up on each side, over the triangle.
Open the shape from the bottom and press it flat into a diamond.
Fold the bottom point of the diamond up to the top, on each side, to make a small triangle.
Open it again from the bottom and press it flat into a smaller diamond.
Gently pull the two top points apart, and the boat will open out.
Float it together in a basin of water, or set it on a shelf to keep.
safety: Use only a few inches of water in a basin or tray, and stay with anyone near water.
Mop up spills straight away so the floor does not become slippery.
Paper edges can give small cuts; fold with the flat of the hand if skin is fragile.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop halfway. A folded triangle is a paper hat, which is a fine result on its own, and you can finish the boat another day or not at all.

cards.name: Fold towels together
cards.summary: Fold warm towels from the dryer together and stack them, with no wrong way to fold.
materials: A basket of clean, dry towels, warm from the dryer
A large flat table, counter or bed to fold on
A laundry basket or cupboard for the finished pile
steps: Sit at a table, or stand at a counter, with the basket of towels beside you.
Lift one towel from the basket and shake it out once.
Bring one edge across to meet the opposite edge.
Smooth the towel flat with both hands.
Fold it in half, or in thirds, however they like.
Place the folded towel on the pile.
Repeat with the next towel, and swap jobs whenever they like.
Stack the finished towels in the laundry basket or cupboard.
safety: Check towels are warm, not hot, before handing them over. Test with the inside of your wrist first.
Before folding, check each towel for pins, loose buttons or other small items that could be dropped or swallowed.
If standing, keep the floor clear of dropped towels and pets, and keep a chair close so they can sit whenever they like.
Keep towels away from stove burners, space heaters and open flames.
Stay with the person while they fold, and remove any pin or button before it can be dropped or swallowed.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one towel. Leave the rest in the basket, or stack what is folded and sit together for a while.

cards.name: Give a hand massage
cards.summary: Gently massage one hand with a little plain lotion, asking first and stopping whenever they wish.
materials: A small bottle of plain, unscented lotion or hand cream
A clean, soft towel to rest the hand on
A chair with arms, or a pillow to support the arm
A bowl of warm water and a towel for washing hands first (optional)
steps: Wash and dry your hands, then sit beside them with the lotion and towel in reach.
Ask if they would like a hand massage, and wait for a clear yes.
Ask which hand they would like to start with, and rest it on the towel.
Warm a small drop of lotion between your palms.
Rest your hands lightly around theirs, without gripping.
Stroke slowly from the wrist toward the knuckles, on the back of the hand.
Move to each finger in turn, with light, slow pressure.
Ask how it feels, and stop straight away if they pull away.
Wipe any extra lotion with the towel, and let the hand rest.
safety: Ask permission before touching, and stop as soon as they pull away, tense up or say to stop.
Test a small drop of plain lotion on the inside of the wrist first, and check for known allergies or skin reactions.
Do not press on red, swollen, bruised, broken or very thin skin. A dry, gentle wipe is enough there.
Avoid sore joints, and never bend fingers past the point where they move easily.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one hand, or even one finger. Wipe the hand dry, rest it on the towel, and sit quietly together.

cards.name: Hold a sing-along at home
cards.summary: Play or sing a few songs they choose, and join in however they like: singing, humming, clapping or just listening.
materials: A phone, radio, tablet or music player, or just your own voices
A comfortable seat for each person
A speaker, if you have one
steps: Sit together somewhere comfortable, with the music player within reach.
Ask what kind of music they would like today, or offer two choices.
Play the first tune, or start humming one they name, at a comfortable volume.
Join in however they like: sing, hum, clap, sway or just listen.
Let the tune finish. Do not fill the quiet, and do not ask anyone to sing a particular part.
Ask whether they would like another, and choose it together.
Stop after a few tunes, or sooner if they have had enough.
safety: Set the volume low and check it with them. Sudden loud sound can startle or hurt.
Check hearing aids are in and working. Turn off autoplay and ads so the music does not change suddenly.
No one is tested on the words. Never ask for a missing line or correct a wrong one.
If a tune seems to upset them, change it or stop. Their choice comes first.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one tune. Turn the music off, sit quietly together, or offer a cup of tea. Try again another day if they would like.

cards.name: Look through a photo album
cards.summary: Turn the pages of a family photo album together, pausing to talk about what is in each picture.
materials: A photo album, or a folder of printed photos you have chosen
Copies of old or fragile prints, if you have them
Tissues and a glass of water within reach
Reading glasses, a magnifier or a lamp, if they help
steps: Sit side by side at a table, or with a lap tray, with the album in easy reach.
Check that glasses are on and the light is bright enough to see the pictures clearly.
Let them open the album to any page they like.
Ask an open question, such as "What can you see here?" or "Tell me about this one."
Listen to what they say, and accept it without checking or correcting it.
Turn the page only when they are ready, or ask whether they would like to turn it.
If a picture brings up sadness, pause, offer a tissue and sit quietly together.
Close the album gently when they are ready, and rest your hand on the cover.
safety: Some photos bring up sadness or loss. Keep tissues close and do not push a conversation that is upsetting them.
Handle old prints with clean, dry hands, and use copies for fragile or valuable photos.
Keep the album on a steady surface so it cannot slide off a lap or tray.
Check photos for addresses or other private details before showing them to visitors or sharing them online.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one page. Close the album, leave it on the table, and talk about something else or sit quietly together.

cards.name: Make a beaded keyring
cards.summary: Thread a few large beads onto a cord, tie it off and fasten it to a keyring to carry or give.
materials: Three to five large beads with big holes
Strong string or cord, about 12 inches long
A split keyring
Clear tape to stiffen one end of the cord
Scissors for the helper only
A tray with raised edges
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the cord to about 12 inches, and wraps one end in clear tape.
Tie a loose knot in the other end of the cord so the beads stay on.
Place the beads in the tray, inside the raised edges, in front of the person.
Slide one bead at a time onto the taped end, counting as you go.
Stop when the beads fill about half the cord, leaving a few inches free.
Tie a firm knot at the free end, so the beads cannot slide off.
Loop the knotted end through the split keyring, and tie a knot to hold it.
Put the beads back in the tray, and count them out and back in.
safety: Beads and small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three and for anyone who mouths things. Do not use beads with an under-three or with anyone who mouths objects.
Use large beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep loose beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Keep the cord short, and do not hang the keyring round a neck or leave it where an under-three can reach it.
Do not use resin or epoxy to hold or seal beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.
Scissors are for the helper only.
An adult stays nearby, and checks every knot before the keyring is used so that no bead can come loose.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop with a few beads on the cord. Tie a knot, put the beads back in the tray and count them, and finish another day, or leave it as it is.

cards.name: Make a button picture
cards.summary: Sort buttons by color or size and glue them onto card to make a simple picture.
materials: A small number of large buttons, about the size of a quarter or bigger
A sheet of thick card, about letter size
White craft glue or a glue dot sheet
A pencil for a simple outline, such as a tree or a flower
A shallow tray or plate to hold the buttons
steps: Count the buttons onto the tray before you start and note the number.
Draw a simple outline on the card together, or choose a shape you like.
Look through the buttons together and sort a few by color or size if they enjoy it.
Ask where the first button should go. Any place is the right one.
Add a dot of glue and press the button down together.
Keep adding buttons, taking turns choosing and placing.
Leave the picture flat to dry somewhere safe.
Count the loose buttons back into their container and check the number matches.
safety: Buttons are a choking hazard. Skip this activity if the person may put small objects in their mouth; use paper circles instead.
Use large buttons only, keep the number small, and count them in and out so none go missing.
To reduce the risk further, glue the buttons onto the card yourself first and use the activity for arranging and talking.
Stay at the table the whole time; do not leave loose buttons within reach of the person or young children.
Use a glue stick or white craft glue rather than hot glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two buttons. Count the loose ones away, leave the picture to dry, and offer to add more another day.

cards.name: Make a color collage
cards.summary: Choose one color, tear out magazine pieces in that color and glue them onto card.
materials: Old magazines, catalogs or colored paper
A sheet of thick card, about letter size
A glue stick
Scissors for the helper, only if cutting is needed
steps: Clear a table, then lay out the card, the glue stick and a pile of magazines.
Choose one color together, such as blue, yellow or green. Any choice is fine.
Turn the pages and find pictures or patches in that color, then tear out the ones you like.
Tear each piece into a rough shape, since torn edges look softer than cut ones.
Glue the back of one piece and press it onto the card.
Keep adding pieces and let them overlap, so the color builds up.
Stop when the card feels full, then press it flat under a heavy book for a few minutes.
safety: Tearing is the main method, so scissors stay with the helper.
Use a glue stick, which is less messy than liquid glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Torn paper edges can nick fingers. Check hands at the end, and wipe glue from the fingers.
Keep small pieces of paper away from the mouth.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a handful of pieces. Leave the card on the table where it is easy to see, and carry on another time or simply enjoy the color.

cards.name: Make a family tree of hands
cards.summary: Trace family members' hands in pencil around a drawn trunk to make a shared tree.
materials: A large sheet of paper or poster board
A pencil for tracing
Colored pencils, crayons or markers for coloring in
A brown marker or crayon for the trunk
Masking tape to hold the paper still
steps: Tape the paper to the table and draw a simple tree trunk and branches together.
Ask who would like to go first. Anyone may choose not to be traced.
Rest one person's hand flat on the paper near a branch, fingers spread comfortably.
Trace around the hand gently with a pencil.
Write that person's name inside or beside the hand.
Repeat for each person who wants to join, taking turns.
Color in the hands together, one color or many, as you like.
Hang or keep the tree somewhere everyone can see it.
safety: Trace with a pencil only and never put paint or ink on skin. Some skin bruises or tears easily, so trace gently and lift away from the hand.
Ask before touching anyone's hand. If spreading fingers is painful, trace the hand relaxed or as a mitten shape.
Family trees can bring up people who have died, separation or estrangement. Include anyone they want and let them lead.
Keep markers away from skin; washable markers come off with soap and water.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one hand. Add more names whenever family visits, or keep the tree as it is. Every version is complete.

cards.name: Make a festival decoration
cards.summary: Make a paper lantern, star, garland or card for a celebration the two of you choose, in your own way.
materials: Colored paper, wrapping paper or old cards, in colors they like
Scissors for the helper
A glue stick or removable tape
Pens, crayons or markers for decorating
String or ribbon for hanging
steps: Ask which celebration or season they would like to make something for, from any tradition or none.
Offer ideas such as a lantern, star, garland, New Year card or harvest or spring decoration, and let them choose or suggest one.
Before starting, if a symbol is sacred to them, ask whether they want it made as a craft, and choose something else if not.
Lay out paper in colors that suit the celebration and let them pick the ones they like.
The helper cuts the paper to size. Fold, roll or loop it together into the chosen shape.
Glue or tape the pieces where needed. They press and hold while you secure it.
Decorate with pens or crayons, adding patterns, symbols or words they choose.
Choose where to hang or stand it, and hang it together with string or ribbon.
safety: Keep scissors with the helper, and put them away between steps.
Do not use candles or real flames, in or near the decoration. Hang paper away from heaters, lamps and stoves.
Check for sensitivity to glue, tape or marker fumes. Use a glue stick and keep the room ventilated.
Hang it where it will not catch on a walker, wheelchair or feet. Use a steady step stool, never a chair.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop at any point. A half-made lantern or a single star is still lovely, and you can come back to it, or put it away, whenever they wish.

cards.name: Make a friendship bracelet
cards.summary: Braid three thick strands of yarn into a simple bracelet or bookmark tassel, taped to the table.
materials: Three colors of thick yarn or embroidery thread, each cut by the helper to about 16 inches long
Scissors for the helper only
Masking tape to hold the strands to the table
A clipboard or a tray for a lap
steps: Lay the three strands side by side and tie one loose knot at the top, leaving a tail of about two inches.
Tape the knot to the table or tray so it stays still.
Spread the three strands apart, with one on each side and one in the middle.
Take the right strand and lay it over the middle one.
Take the left strand and lay it over the new middle one.
Keep going, right over middle, then left over middle, pulling each strand snug but not tight.
When the braid is long enough to go around the wrist or lie in a book, tie a loose knot at the end.
Trim the ends to a short tassel, or tie the bracelet around a wrist loosely. The helper does the trimming.
safety: Scissors are for the helper only. Cut the strands before you start and put the scissors away.
Keep strands short, never wrap yarn around a neck, and take a bracelet off if it feels tight. Keep long strands away from the neck.
Loose ends can be swallowed or chewed. Supervise if anyone might put yarn or tassel ends in the mouth.
Choose soft yarn that does not itch or irritate sensitive skin, and gather up loose yarn so nobody trips on it.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop whenever you like. Tape the end down, leave the braid on the table, and pick it up another day, or leave it as a short bookmark.

cards.name: Make a greeting card
cards.summary: A folded card with a picture on the front and a short message inside, made for someone you both know.
materials: A sheet of thick paper or card, folded in half
Pictures cut from old cards, magazines or seed packets
A glue stick
A thick felt-tip pen or marker
An envelope
steps: Talk together about who the card is for, such as a grandchild, a neighbor or an old friend.
Lay out four or five pictures and ask which one suits that person.
Glue the chosen picture to the front of the folded card.
Open the card and ask what they would like to say. A few words are plenty.
Write the message, or let them write it if they prefer.
Ask whether they would like to sign it, add a mark, or have you sign for both of you.
Put the card in the envelope and agree together when to send or deliver it.
safety: If you cut pictures, keep the scissors with the helper.
A glue stick is less messy than liquid glue; check for skin sensitivity first.
Do not ask anyone to write if it is tiring or upsetting. Dictating the message counts fully.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop with just a picture on the front. Keep the card in a safe place and finish the message another day, or send it as it is.

cards.name: Make a lavender sachet
cards.summary: Spoon dried lavender onto a square of fabric and tie it into a small scented bundle.
materials: A square of cotton fabric, about 8 inches across
Two or three spoonfuls of dried lavender
A ribbon or piece of yarn, about 12 inches
A small bowl and a teaspoon
A tray or plate to catch spills
steps: Set the tray on the table and pour the lavender into the bowl.
Offer the bowl to smell, and ask if they would like to make a sachet with it.
Lay the fabric square flat on the tray, patterned side down.
Spoon lavender into the middle of the fabric together.
Gather the four corners up into a small bundle.
Hold the bundle while one person wraps the ribbon around the neck.
Tie the ribbon in a knot or a bow. The helper can do this.
Decide together where the sachet should go, such as a drawer or a coat pocket.
safety: Strong scents can be unpleasant or trigger headaches or breathing problems for some people. Smell a little first and stop if anyone dislikes it.
Some people react to lavender on the skin. Use a spoon and wash hands afterward if there is any sensitivity.
Dried lavender and rice are small enough to swallow. Supervise closely if anything might be put in the mouth.
Do not put the sachet near a heater, radiator or open flame.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop at any point. A bowl of lavender to smell is enough on its own. Cover the bowl and offer to finish the sachet another day.

cards.name: Make a memory collage
cards.summary: A relaxed creative activity using photos, magazine pictures and paper.
materials: A few printed photos or copies (never the only print)
Old magazines, calendars or seed catalogs
A sheet of thick paper or card, about letter size
A glue stick
Scissors for the helper
steps: Clear a table and lay out the paper, the glue stick and a small pile of pictures.
Look through the pictures together and talk about any that catch an eye.
Ask which picture should go in the middle. Any answer is the right one.
Glue the back of that picture and press it down together.
Add more pictures around it, taking turns choosing and placing.
Stop when it feels finished, or when you have had enough for today.
Agree on a place to keep or show the collage, such as a fridge or a frame.
safety: Keep scissors with the helper if cutting is unsafe or tiring.
Use copies of photos so an original is never cut or glued by mistake.
A glue stick is less messy than liquid glue; check for skin sensitivity first.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one picture. Put the collage somewhere safe and offer to carry on another day, or simply enjoy looking at the pictures.

cards.name: Make a paper chain garland
cards.summary: A long garland of looped paper strips, made one link at a time and hung up to brighten a room.
materials: Colored paper, wrapping paper or old magazine pages
Scissors for the helper, or a paper trimmer
A glue stick or a stapler for the helper
A ruler and pencil
Removable tape or hooks for hanging
steps: Cut paper into strips about one inch wide and eight inches long before you begin.
Lay the strips out and ask which colors or patterns to use.
Bend one strip into a loop and glue or tape the ends together.
Thread the next strip through the first loop.
Close the second loop, so the two links are joined.
Keep adding links, taking turns or with one person threading and the other closing.
Hold the chain up together now and then to see how long it has grown.
Decide together where to hang it, such as a window, a doorway or across a mantel.
safety: Keep scissors, staplers and paper trimmers with the helper.
Hang the finished garland well away from candles, heaters and lamps.
Hang it high enough that it will not catch on walkers, wheelchairs or feet, and use a steady step stool, not a chair.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few links. A short chain still looks cheerful on a doorknob, and you can add to it any time; it never needs to be finished.

cards.name: Make a personal songbook
cards.summary: Collect favorite songs, a few lines of words and the stories behind them in one book.
materials: A notebook or a few sheets of paper in a folder
A pen or a thick marker
A phone, radio or music player to play songs
Printed lyrics for a few songs (optional)
Old record sleeves, sheet music or concert programs, if you have them
steps: Sit together and open the book to a blank page.
Ask about a song they enjoy, or offer a choice of two familiar songs.
Play the song at a comfortable volume and listen together.
Write the song title at the top of the page.
Add the singer or a favorite line, if they want to.
Invite a story about the song, such as where they heard it or who they danced with.
Write a few words about the story, in their words.
Play the song again if they would like, or choose the next one.
safety: Keep the volume comfortable and check it with them. Sudden loud music can startle or hurt.
Check hearing aids are in, switched on and not whistling. Some people prefer headphones off and the speaker nearby.
Some songs bring back sad memories or people who have died. Pause, listen kindly, and offer another song or a break.
Avoid songs with lyrics or associations that may upset them; follow their lead on what to play.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one song. Leave the book open at that page, play something gentle, or simply sit and listen together for a while.

cards.name: Make a photo postcard
cards.summary: Glue a copy of a favorite photo onto card, then write one line together.
materials: A copy of a favorite photo, printed or photocopied. Never use the only print.
A postcard-sized piece of thick card, or a blank postcard
A glue stick
A pen with a thick grip
An envelope, a stamp and the address, if sending
steps: Look through the photo copies together and choose one to send.
Place the photo on the card to see how it fits, and ask the helper to trim it if needed.
Glue the back of the photo and press it onto the card.
Press the photo flat with a hand and hold it for a few seconds.
Ask who the card is for, and what one line they would like to write.
Write the line on the back of the card, in the words the person chooses, and sign it together.
If sending, put the card in an envelope with the address and a stamp.
safety: Use photo copies only, so an original is never cut, glued or lost.
Use a glue stick, which is less messy than liquid glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Check the address before sealing the envelope. Never write bank details or passwords on a card.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after choosing the photo. Keep the copy somewhere handy and carry on another day, or simply look at it together.

cards.name: Make a pine cone bird feeder
cards.summary: Spread fat on a pine cone, roll it in birdseed and hang it outside to watch the birds.
materials: A large, open, dry pine cone
Vegetable shortening, or peanut butter if nobody has a nut allergy
Wild birdseed in a shallow dish
A blunt knife or spoon for spreading
String or garden twine, about 18 inches
Newspaper or a tray to work on
Wet wipes or a damp cloth
steps: Cover the table and set out the pine cone, the fat and the dish of seed.
Tie the string around the top of the pine cone. The helper can do this.
Spread fat into the gaps of the cone with the spoon or knife.
Roll the cone in the dish of seed together, pressing it in.
Sprinkle any bare patches with more seed by hand.
Choose a branch or hook that can be seen from a window or chair.
Hang the feeder there together, or let them watch while you hang it.
Sit by the window and see which birds arrive, if you like.
safety: Peanut butter can cause a severe allergic reaction. Ask about nut allergies first, and use vegetable shortening if anyone is unsure.
Birdseed is not food for people, and small seeds can be a choking risk. Supervise if anything might be put in the mouth.
Keep any knife blunt, or use a spoon. Wash hands after handling seed and fat.
Hang the feeder from the ground or a stable step, never a chair or ladder. Keep paths clear outdoors to prevent falls.
Pine cones collected outdoors can have sharp scales and sap. Choose dry, open ones and check them first.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop once the cone has a little seed on it. The birds will not mind. Hang it as it is, or leave it on a tray and finish another day.

cards.name: Make a playlist together
cards.summary: Choose a few favorite songs together on a phone, play each one and write the ones they like on a card.
materials: A phone, tablet or music player with a few songs saved, or a music service set up in advance
A small card, index card or sheet of paper
A thick pen or marker
Headphones or a small speaker, if you have them
steps: Sit together with the phone, the card and the pen in reach.
Ask what kind of music they enjoy, or offer two familiar styles to choose from.
Find one song they name, or pick one from the choices you offered.
Play the song at a comfortable volume and listen together.
Ask whether they like it.
Write the title on the card if they say yes.
Choose the next song together, and repeat until the card has five to eight titles.
Read the list aloud and ask which song they would like to hear first.
safety: Set the volume low and check it with them. Sudden loud music can startle or hurt.
Check hearing aids are in and working. Use headphones only if they fit comfortably and do not pinch the ears.
Some songs bring back sad memories. Pause, listen kindly, and offer another song or a break.
Turn off autoplay video and ads before you start, so the music does not change to something unexpected.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two songs. Leave the card as it is, play something gentle, or simply sit and listen together for a while.

cards.name: Make a sealed shaker
cards.summary: Fill a small sealed bottle with dried rice, decorate it and shake along to a favorite song.
materials: A small clean plastic bottle with a screw-on lid, such as a juice or water bottle, empty and dry
A small handful of dried rice
A funnel, or a folded piece of paper to guide the rice
Craft glue and strong tape for sealing the lid
Colored tape, paper or stickers for decoration
A phone or player with a steady song
steps: Sit at a table with the bottle, rice, funnel and decorations in reach.
Pour in a small handful of rice, enough to fill about a quarter of the bottle.
Ask the helper to glue the lid shut, then wrap tape firmly over it.
Decorate the outside with tape, paper or stickers, one piece at a time, while the glue dries.
Leave the shaker to dry fully, overnight if possible, and check the lid is firm.
Next time, play a song and hold the shaker so it is easy to move.
Shake gently in time with the beat, then try a slower shake.
Set the shaker down and store it out of reach of anyone who puts things in their mouth.
safety: Glue the lid shut and tape over it, then check the lid before each use. Replace the shaker if the lid loosens or the bottle cracks.
Never make or use this with someone who puts things in their mouth. Keep the shaker away from anyone who may chew or swallow small grains.
Fill with dried rice only. Do not add small beads, coins, buttons or other small items, which can be swallowed.
Sweep up spilled rice at once, because loose grains on the floor are a slip hazard.
Stay close while the shaker is used, and keep it out of reach of anyone who may put it in their mouth.
Check for food allergies before using rice or any grain, and wash hands after handling it.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after the first shake, or before the decoration is finished. Put the shaker on the shelf and finish it another day.

cards.name: Make a texture board
cards.summary: Glue different textures onto a sturdy board to make something interesting to touch and look at.
materials: A piece of sturdy cardboard, about letter size
Six to ten textured scraps: corduroy, felt, velvet, burlap, ribbon, sponge
A few household textures, such as a bottle cap, a button or a strip of bubble wrap
White craft glue or a hot glue gun for the helper
Scissors for the helper
steps: Lay the textured scraps out on the table in a row.
Pass each one over and feel it together, saying what it is like if you wish.
Ask which texture they would like to put on the board first.
Spread glue on the back of that piece. The helper can do this.
Press it onto the board together and hold for a few seconds.
Add more pieces, taking turns choosing where each one goes.
Leave the board flat to dry, as the glue bottle suggests.
Run your hands across the finished board together and talk about favorites.
safety: Glue all pieces firmly. Buttons, caps and beads are choking risks if they come loose and might be put in the mouth.
If small pieces might be mouthed, leave out buttons and caps and use only large fabric pieces.
Keep any hot glue gun and scissors with the helper. Let hot glue cool fully before the board is handled.
Avoid sharp edges such as cut plastic, wire or sandpaper; check the board by hand before handing it over.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one or two pieces. Feeling the scraps together is the activity too. Set the board aside to finish later, or keep it as it is.

cards.name: Make a tissue paper window picture
cards.summary: Press torn pieces of colored tissue paper onto clear sticky film, then hang it in a window to let light shine through.
materials: Clear self-adhesive film (contact film), cut by the helper to about letter size
Colored tissue paper, torn beforehand into pieces about the size of a palm
Two or three shallow bowls to sort the colors
Masking tape, for the helper to hold the film and to hang it
Scissors, for the helper to use beforehand only
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the film to size, peels off the backing and tapes it sticky side up to the table.
Put the bowls of tissue pieces within easy reach.
Choose a color together. Any color is a good one.
Pick up a piece and press it onto the sticky film anywhere you like.
Add more pieces, and let them overlap so the colors mix.
Stop when the picture feels full or you are ready to be done.
The helper lays a second piece of film over the top or folds the first one in half, and smooths it down.
Hang the picture in a window and look at the light coming through.
safety: The helper cuts the film with scissors beforehand and puts them away. The person does not cut anything.
Keep small torn tissue pieces and the film away from the mouth, and stay nearby while they are out. Clear them away afterward.
Check for sensitivity to the sticky film or tape, and keep the sticky side off bare skin and hair.
The helper hangs the picture, using a stable chair or step stool if needed. The person does not climb or lean out.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop with only a few pieces on the film. A sparse picture lets in plenty of light, and you can add more another day.

cards.name: Make a torn paper landscape
cards.summary: Tear long strips of colored paper and layer them into sky, hills and ground.
materials: Scrap paper in blues, greens and browns, such as old envelopes, wrapping paper or painted scrap
A sheet of card or thick paper, about letter size
A glue stick
A tray or box lid to hold the torn strips
steps: Lay the card flat in front of the person, with the long side across if they prefer.
Tear a few long strips of pale blue or white paper for the sky and place them in a tray.
Tear strips in greens for hills, and strips in browns or yellows for the ground.
Rub glue on the top third of the card and press the sky strips on, letting them overlap.
Glue the middle of the card and press on the green strips, tearing a wavy edge along the top for hills.
Glue the bottom and add the ground strips, overlapping the bottom of the hills.
Add a torn round of yellow paper for a sun, or a few small green scraps for trees, if wanted.
Press the picture flat with a clean hand and leave it to dry, then choose where to put it.
safety: Use a glue stick rather than liquid glue, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Torn paper edges can nick fingers. Offer softer paper if that is a concern, and wipe glue from the fingers.
Keep small torn scraps away from anyone who may put paper in their mouth, and clear them away afterward.
Supervise closely while small torn scraps are on the table.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after the sky or after a few strips. A picture with only sky and one hill still looks good, and you can add more another day or leave it as it is.

cards.name: Make leaf rubbings
cards.summary: Lay leaves under thin paper and rub with the side of a crayon until the veins appear.
materials: A few leaves with clear veins from a garden, a park or a houseplant, such as maple, oak, ivy or a geranium
Thin paper, such as copy paper or tracing paper
Wax crayons with the paper wrapper peeled off, used on their sides
A tray or a clipboard
Low-tack masking tape to hold the paper still
steps: Set out the leaves, paper and crayons on a tray or at the table.
Choose a leaf together and look at it. Any leaf is a good leaf.
Lay the leaf vein-side up on the tray.
Cover the leaf with a sheet of paper and tape the paper corners to the tray so it stays still.
Peel the wrapper off a crayon and hold it flat, on its side.
Rub gently over the leaf in one direction until the veins and edge come up.
Lift the paper to look. Try a second leaf, or the same leaf in another color.
Lay the finished rubbings side by side to look at together.
safety: Use leaves from a garden, a park or a houseplant that you know. Do not pick wild plants that could be poisonous, and avoid poison ivy, poison oak and sumac.
Check for plant allergies and skin sensitivity before handling leaves, and wash hands afterward.
Keep leaves and crayons away from the mouth. Do not let anyone chew or taste them.
Use low-tack tape on the paper only, and take it off gently so the paper does not tear.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one leaf. Leave the rubbing on the table to look at, or take a short look at the plants nearby if you would like to.

cards.name: Match colors to a tune
cards.summary: Listen to a short tune together, then pick the colors that seem to go with it and lay them in a row.
materials: A phone, radio or music player
Three or four short tunes they like, in different styles
Squares of colored paper about the size of a hand, or paint sample cards
A tray or a sheet of plain paper to lay the colors on
steps: Spread the colored squares on the table where they can see them all.
Ask which tune they would like first, or offer two to choose from.
Play the tune at a comfortable volume and listen together.
When it ends, ask which color seems to go with it, and let them pick one or a few.
Lay the chosen colors in a row on the tray. Any color is a good answer.
Play the next tune and start a new row beside the first.
Look at the rows together, and keep the one they like best if they wish.
safety: Keep the volume low and check it with them. A sudden loud sound can startle.
Turn off autoplay and ads so the music does not change without warning.
There is no right color for a tune. Never correct a choice or ask them to explain it.
If a tune upsets them, stop it and choose another, or end there.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one tune. Leave the row of colors on the tray, turn the music off and sit together for a while.

cards.name: Move to music in a chair
cards.summary: Move gently in a chair to a tune they choose: tap feet, sway, roll shoulders or wave a scarf to the beat.
materials: A tune they choose, saved on a phone or player, or a song you can sing together
A sturdy chair without wheels, with arms if they prefer
A light scarf or a strip of soft cloth, if they like
Clear floor space around the chair
steps: Set a sturdy chair with no wheels on a flat, clear floor, with nothing to trip over around it.
Ask what tune they would like. Offer two or three choices, or let them pick their own.
Help them sit back with both feet flat on the floor, and play the tune at a comfortable volume.
Start with something small, such as tapping one foot or a hand on the knee, and let them copy or lead.
Try one movement at a time: sway side to side, roll the shoulders, or reach a scarf up and down.
Move at their pace and in their way. There is no right shape and nothing to count.
Move along with them, and follow any movement they come up with.
Let the song end, then sit quietly together and offer a drink of water.
safety: Keep them seated in a stable chair with no wheels, feet flat on the floor. Do not ask them to stand up and dance.
Pain means stop. Never ask for more movement than they offer, and do not count repetitions.
This is not exercise or rehabilitation. Check with their doctor or care team before any new movement.
Stay within arm's reach and keep the space around the chair clear. Keep the scarf away from the neck.
Pause if they look tired, short of breath or unsteady, and offer a drink of water.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one song, or after a few bars. Turn the music down, sit quietly together and say that was lovely, or simply that is enough for now.

cards.name: Paint a garden stone
cards.summary: A smooth stone painted with simple colors or patterns, then placed outdoors where you both can see it.
materials: A few smooth, flat stones about the size of a palm
Non-toxic, water-based acrylic or poster paint
Brushes with thick handles, or cotton swabs for dots
A jar of water and paper towels
Newspaper or an old cloth to cover the table
A water-based outdoor varnish, applied by the helper (optional)
steps: Wash the stones and let them dry before you start.
Set out two or three stones and ask which one they would like to paint.
Pick one or two colors together.
Paint a base color over the top of the stone, or leave the natural stone showing.
Add a simple pattern if you both like, such as dots, stripes, a flower or a single initial.
Leave the stone to dry for about an hour, then add a second coat if you want stronger color.
Choose a spot together where the stone will sit, such as a flower bed, a doorstep or a window ledge.
Carry the stone out and place it, or have it carried out if walking is tiring.
safety: Use non-toxic, water-based paint; wash it off skin with soap and water, and check for skin sensitivity first.
Choose stones too large to fit in the mouth, and lift heavy ones for the participant.
Outdoors, sit in the shade, offer water and a hat, and keep sessions short on hot or cold days.
If you use varnish, the helper applies it in a ventilated space with no one else nearby.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one color. A plain painted stone looks good in a garden, and you can add a pattern another day or leave it exactly as it is.

cards.name: Paint a shared picture
cards.summary: Paint one large picture together, with everyone adding a mark in turn.
materials: A large sheet of thick paper, or several sheets taped edge to edge
Non-toxic, water-based paint or washable poster paint in several colors
Brushes, sponges and a few cotton swabs
A cup of water for each person
A plastic tablecloth or old towels under the paper
Masking tape and paper towels
steps: Cover the table with a plastic cloth, then tape the large paper flat over it at all four corners.
Set out the paints, brushes and water cups so everyone can reach them.
Ask each person what to begin with, such as a sky, a shape, a line or a color. Any choice is fine.
Let everyone make a first mark anywhere on the paper.
Take turns adding one mark or shape at a time, and pause to look at the whole picture between turns.
Rinse the brush in the water cup before changing color.
Stop when the picture feels finished, then leave it flat to dry.
When the paint is dry, remove the tape and choose a place to hang the picture.
safety: Use non-toxic, water-based paint only, and check for any known paint allergies first.
Keep brushes and small items away from the mouth, and do not let anyone drink from the water cups.
Put towels or a plastic cloth under the paper, and wipe up spills at once so no one slips.
Wash hands after painting, and keep paint away from the face if skin is sensitive.
Stay close while paint and brushes are in use, and keep the water cups out of reach of anyone who may drink from them.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one mark. Leave the picture where it is, and carry on another time, or simply enjoy the marks made so far.

cards.name: Paint with watercolors
cards.summary: Loose, colorful washes of watercolor paint on paper, where blending and running colors are the whole point.
materials: A non-toxic, water-based watercolor set
Two medium brushes with thick handles
Thick paper or watercolor paper
Two jars or cups of clean water
An old towel or newspaper to cover the table
Paper towels for blotting
steps: Cover the table with the towel or newspaper and set out the paint, brushes and water.
Ask which two or three colors they would like to use today.
Brush clean water over the whole sheet of paper together.
Dip a brush in one color and touch it to the wet paper.
Watch together as the color spreads, then add a second color next to it.
Tilt the paper gently if you both want the colors to run and mix.
Talk about what the shapes look like, such as a sky, a field or nothing at all.
Leave the painting flat to dry and decide together whether to paint another.
safety: Use only non-toxic, water-based paint, and keep the painting water separate from any drinking cups.
Some people put brushes in their mouth; stay close and use clearly different cups for paint water and drinks.
Wash paint off skin with warm water and soap, and check first for any skin sensitivity.
Wipe up spilled water promptly so floors do not become slippery.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one wash of color. Leave the paper to dry somewhere flat and offer to paint again another day, or simply look at it together.

cards.name: Plant seeds in a pot
cards.summary: Fill a pot with soil, press in a few large seeds and water them together.
materials: A small plant pot with a drainage hole and a saucer
Bagged potting mix
A few large seeds, such as beans, peas, nasturtiums or sunflowers
A spoon or small trowel
A small watering can or a cup of water
Gardening gloves, if wanted
Newspaper or a tray to work on
steps: Spread newspaper or a tray on the table and set the pot on it.
Spoon potting mix into the pot together until it is nearly full.
Press the soil down gently with flat hands.
Show the seeds and ask which ones they would like to plant.
Push each seed into the soil about as deep as a fingertip.
Cover the seeds with a little soil and pat it down.
Water slowly together until the soil looks dark and damp.
Choose a bright windowsill for the pot and agree who will check on it.
safety: Wear gloves or wash hands after handling potting mix; it can contain bacteria and fungi, and some mixes include fertilizer.
Seeds can be a choking risk and many are treated with chemicals. Supervise closely if anything might be put in the mouth.
Some seeds, such as sweet peas, are toxic if eaten. Read the packet and choose edible-garden seeds if unsure.
Outdoors, sit in the shade, offer water to drink, and keep the path clear of hoses and tools to prevent falls.
Check for allergies to seeds or plants before handling them, and wash hands afterward.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one seed. Water what is planted, put the pot somewhere bright, and finish another day if you both want to.

cards.name: Press leaves and flowers
cards.summary: Gather flat leaves and flowers, then press them between paper in a heavy book together.
materials: A handful of flat leaves and small flowers, checked as safe to handle
A large, heavy book you do not mind marking
Plain paper, paper towels or coffee filters
A few more books or a brick to add weight
A small basket or bag for collecting
steps: Walk outside together or bring a few leaves and flowers to the table.
Lay them out and look at the shapes and colors together.
Ask which ones they would like to keep. Flat, dry pieces press best.
Open the book near the middle and lay a sheet of paper on the page.
Place the leaves and flowers on the paper with a little space between them.
Lay a second sheet of paper on top.
Close the book gently and stack the other books on top.
Write the date on a slip of paper and tuck it in the cover.
Agree on a day, about two weeks away, to open the book together.
safety: Some plants are toxic or irritate skin, such as foxglove, poison ivy and giant hogweed. Check every plant you pick and wash hands afterward.
Avoid holly, roses with thorns, and prickly or stinging plants.
Dried petals and seed heads are small enough to swallow. Supervise if anything might be put in the mouth.
Outdoors, choose level paths, wear sturdy shoes, and take a hat and water in the sun.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one leaf. Close the book on whatever is in it, and you will still have something to open together later.

cards.name: Print with leaves
cards.summary: Paint the back of a leaf, press it onto paper and lift it to reveal the printed veins.
materials: Fallen leaves with clear veins, such as maple, fern or hosta
Non-toxic, water-based paint or washable ink in one or two colors
A small brush or a sponge
Thick paper or card
Newspaper or a plastic cloth, and paper towels
steps: Cover the table with newspaper or a plastic cloth, and set out the paper, paint and brush.
Choose a leaf together and look at its veins. Any leaf is a good leaf.
Lay the leaf vein-side up on the newspaper.
Paint a thin, even layer over the veins with the brush.
Turn the leaf over and press it paint-side down onto the paper, then press gently all over with a paper towel.
Lift the leaf slowly from one edge and set it aside.
Let the print dry flat, then choose another leaf and try a different color.
safety: Check every leaf before handling. Avoid poison ivy, poison oak and sumac, and check for allergies.
Use non-toxic, water-based paint, and wash hands afterward.
Keep leaves and paint away from the mouth, and do not let anyone chew or taste the plants.
Pick up only fallen leaves, and never strip a living plant.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one leaf. Leave the print flat to dry and carry on later, or go for a short look at the trees nearby.

cards.name: Print with sponge shapes
cards.summary: Press a thick sponge shape into paint, then onto paper, and lift it to see the print.
materials: Thick kitchen sponges, cut by the helper into big, simple shapes such as a circle, a square or a leaf
Washable, non-toxic poster paint in two or three colors
Two or three shallow plates to hold the paint
Thick paper or card, plain or folded into a card
Newspaper or a plastic cloth, and paper towels
Scissors, for the helper to use beforehand only
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the sponges into big, simple shapes and puts the scissors away.
Cover the table, then set out the paper and the sponge shapes.
Pour a thin layer of paint onto each plate, one color per plate.
Choose a shape and a color together. Any choice is a good choice.
Press the sponge flat into the paint, then press it onto the paper.
Lift the sponge straight up and look at the print.
Print again in the same place or somewhere new, and change shape or color whenever you like.
Leave the paper flat to dry and choose where to show it.
safety: The helper cuts the sponges with scissors beforehand and puts them away before the person sits down. The person does not cut anything.
Use washable, non-toxic paint, check for skin sensitivity first, and wash hands afterward.
Keep paint and sponge pieces away from the mouth, and stay nearby throughout.
Throw away any trimmings from cutting the sponges, and wipe the table and floor around the plates.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one print. Leave it to dry and put the sponges and paint away, or come back to it another day.

cards.name: Roll paper beads
cards.summary: Roll thin paper triangles around a pencil or straw to make colorful beads, then thread them on a string.
materials: Old magazine pages, or colored paper, for the strips
A glue stick
A pencil or a thin drinking straw
Scissors for the helper only
Strong string or cord to thread them on
A tray with raised edges
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the paper into long, thin triangles, about six inches long.
Lay one triangle on the table with the wide end toward you.
Add a line of glue along the narrow end, using the glue stick.
Place the pencil or straw on the wide end, and roll the paper tightly around it.
Press the glued tip down to seal the bead, then slide it off the pencil or straw.
Let the finished beads dry for a few minutes on the table.
Make more beads, and keep them in the tray with raised edges so none roll away.
Thread each dry bead onto the string one at a time, counting each one as it goes on.
Tie a knot at each end of the string, so the beads stay on.
safety: Beads and small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three and for anyone who mouths things. Do not make or use paper beads with an under-three or with anyone who mouths objects.
Use paper beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep the beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Scissors are for the helper only, and the paper is cut away from the hands.
Do not use resin or epoxy to seal or harden beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.
The glue stick is not for eating or mouthing. Let the glue dry before you thread the beads.
An adult stays nearby while the beads are being made and threaded, and the finished string is never worn on the neck.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few beads. Put them in the tray, count them, and finish another day, or leave a half-rolled bead on the table as it is.

cards.name: Shape a pinch pot
cards.summary: Shape a small bowl from air-dry clay by pressing it open with your thumbs.
materials: Air-dry clay, about the size of a tennis ball for each person
A plastic tablecloth or oilcloth to protect the table
A damp cloth or sponge
A small bowl of water
A tray or board on which to leave the finished pot to dry
steps: Cover the table with a plastic cloth and put the damp cloth and the water bowl within reach.
Give each person a ball of clay about the size of a tennis ball.
Roll the clay gently between the palms until the surface is smooth.
Press a thumb into the middle to make a dip, then stop and look at it.
Turn the clay slowly and press the walls out with the thumbs, a little at a time, keeping the base flat.
Keep the walls an even thickness, about as thick as a pencil, and dampen the fingers only when the clay feels dry.
Smooth the rim with a damp finger, then wipe the fingers on the cloth.
Set the finished pot on a tray and leave it to dry for a day or two, away from direct heat.
safety: Use non-toxic air-dry clay, and keep clay and fingers away from the mouth.
Clay can dry out the skin. Keep a bowl of water nearby, and offer hand cream afterward if needed.
Keep the finished pot away from the mouth until it is fully dry, and check the rim for sharp edges.
Wipe up dried clay with a damp cloth rather than sweeping, so no dust is breathed in.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop once the clay feels tiring. Wrap it in a damp cloth inside a plastic bag and carry on another day; stopping early is fine.

cards.name: Sketch what is on the table
cards.summary: Look at one everyday object on the table, then draw its outline with any marks you like.
materials: One simple object, such as a cup, a piece of fruit or a flower in a small vase
Plain paper, about letter size
A soft pencil or a thick marker
A soft eraser, optional
steps: Place the object on the table in front of the person, where the light falls well on it.
Look at it together for a moment, and talk about its color, shape or size if they like.
Put the paper down and place the pencil in their hand, or within easy reach.
Draw the outline with a few slow lines, starting from the bottom edge. Any line is a good line.
Add a few marks inside, such as a line for a handle, a dot for a seed or a stroke for a stem.
Draw your own version beside theirs if you like, without comparing the two.
Stop when they put the pencil down, then look at the drawing together.
safety: If the object is a plant, check that it is not poisonous or an allergen, and do not let anyone taste it.
Keep pencils and erasers away from the mouth if the person may chew or taste things.
Choose a sturdy cup or soft fruit, and avoid glass or anything sharp on the table.
Stay close if the object is small or edible, and do not let anyone eat it.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few lines. Leave the paper where it is and look at the object again later, or simply enjoy it together for a while.

cards.name: Sort a box of postcards
cards.summary: Look through a box of postcards or picture cards together and sort them into piles the person chooses.
materials: A box of postcards or picture cards, 20 to 40 at most
A table, or a firm tray across the lap or on a bed table
Two or three plain plates or sheets of paper to hold the piles
steps: Look through the box first and set aside any card with writing you would rather not read aloud.
Place the box on the table and let them take out a card whenever they like.
Look at the card together and say what you can see, such as a beach, a flower or a bridge.
Offer a plate and ask whether they would like the card on a pile of its own or with another.
Let them choose the piles, such as places, colors or the ones they like best.
Move the card to the pile they choose, and move it again if they change their mind.
Carry on for as long as they enjoy it, and look at a favorite card for a while if they wish.
Put the piles back in the box in any order, or leave a favorite card on the table.
safety: Do not ask them to name, date or explain any card. Looking and choosing is the whole job.
Check that no card has a torn edge, a staple or a small loose sticker before you start.
Keep the box small, so the pile never feels like a task to finish. Stop whenever they lose interest.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one card. Close the box, leave a favorite card where they can see it, and sit together for a while.

cards.name: Sort buttons by color
cards.summary: Sort a bowl of large buttons into a muffin tin or small dishes by color or size, in any order.
materials: A bowl or tub of large buttons, in a few colors or sizes
A muffin tin, or a few small dishes or bowls
A tray or towel to work on
steps: Sit at a table with the bowl of buttons, the muffin tin and the tray in reach.
Pour a small handful of buttons onto the tray.
Pick up one button and look at its color and size.
Place it in a muffin cup or dish that matches, or start a new one.
Keep going, one button at a time, in whatever order they like.
Ask what they notice about the colors or sizes as the dishes fill up.
Tip the buttons back into the bowl, one dish at a time.
safety: Use only large buttons that cannot fit in the mouth, and remove any small or loose parts from the bowl.
Never use this with someone who puts things in their mouth. Stay close and keep the bowl on the table.
Count the buttons out at the start and back in at the end, so none are left on the floor or in a chair.
Check buttons for cracks, sharp edges or loose threads before use, and remove any that are damaged.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few buttons. Tip the sorted buttons back into the bowl, and leave the dishes out for another time.

cards.name: Start a family recipe book
cards.summary: Talk about favorite dishes and write them down together, one page at a time.
materials: A notebook, binder or a few sheets of lined paper
A pen that writes easily
Old recipe cards or cookbooks, if you have them
A few pictures of food from magazines or packaging (optional)
A folder or envelope to keep loose pages together
steps: Sit together at a table with the notebook open to a blank page.
Ask about a dish they liked to make or eat, such as a Sunday meal or a holiday treat.
Write the name of the dish at the top of the page.
Ask what went into it and write the ingredients as a simple list. Rough amounts are fine.
Ask how it was made and write the steps in their own words.
Invite a story, such as who made it, where it was eaten, or what it smelled like.
Read the page back aloud and change anything they want changed.
Stop after one page, or carry on with another dish if you both want to.
safety: This is a writing and talking activity, not cooking. Keep it away from a hot stove or oven, and do not test recipes during the session.
Food memories can bring up people who have died or hard times. Pause, listen, and let them lead, or move to another dish.
There are no wrong answers. If amounts or steps sound unusual, write them as told rather than correcting them.
If you later cook a recipe together, check for allergies, swallowing needs and diet advice first.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a single dish name. Close the book, leave it somewhere easy to find, and offer to add another page on a different day.

cards.name: Tap a rhythm together
cards.summary: Tap along to a steady song on a table or small drum, taking turns to lead the beat.
materials: A song with a clear, steady beat, saved on a phone or player
A table, a tray or the arm of a chair to tap on
A small hand drum, tambourine or pair of wooden blocks, if you have them
A folded towel or cushion to rest the arm on, if needed
steps: Sit where you can both reach the table or tray, with any drum or blocks in front of you.
Choose a song with a steady beat and play it at a comfortable volume.
Listen for a few bars and find the beat together.
Tap the beat gently, with one finger or a flat palm, at a speed that feels comfortable.
Invite them to tap along, copying what you do.
Swap places, so they lead and you copy the tap they choose.
Pause the song whenever they want a rest, and start again when they are ready.
Finish with one last tap together, then rest both hands on the table.
safety: Keep taps gentle and stop if the hands or wrists hurt. Offer a softer surface or a slower song instead.
Use soft drumsticks, fingers or a flat palm. Hard sticks can bruise thin skin.
Keep the volume comfortable and check hearing aids are in and working. Loud bass can startle.
Small blocks can be swallowed. Keep them on the table or tray, and put them away when the activity ends.
Stay close while small blocks or drums are in use, and put them away when the activity ends.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after a few bars. Rest the hands on the table, say that is enough for now, and sit quietly together.

cards.name: Make a torn paper mosaic
cards.summary: A picture built from small pieces of torn colored paper, with no scissors and no right way to place them.
materials: Colored paper, old magazine pages or wrapping paper
A sheet of card, about letter size
A glue stick
A pencil for the outline
Two or three shallow bowls or saucers to sort the pieces
steps: Draw a large, simple shape on the card together, such as a leaf, a house, a fish or a circle.
Tear a few pages into strips, then into pieces about the size of a postage stamp.
Sort the pieces into bowls by color, or leave them mixed if you both prefer.
Rub glue over a small part of the shape.
Press pieces onto the glued area, taking turns or working side by side.
Talk about the colors as you go, such as which ones remind you of a garden, the sea or a favorite coat.
Glue the next small area and keep filling the shape until it feels finished.
Leave it flat to dry and choose a place to show it.
safety: Keep small torn pieces away from anyone who may put paper in their mouth, and clear them away afterward.
Use a glue stick rather than liquid glue; check for skin sensitivity first.
Glossy magazine edges can occasionally nick skin, so offer softer paper if that is a concern.
Supervise closely while small torn pieces are on the table, and clear them away afterward.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop when only part of the shape is filled. A half-finished mosaic still looks good, and you can add more another day or leave it as it is.

cards.name: Thread a large bead bracelet
cards.summary: Slide large beads onto stretchy cord, one at a time, to make a simple bracelet to wear or give.
materials: Large beads with big holes, enough for the bracelet
Stretchy elastic bead cord, about 12 inches long
Clear tape to stiffen one end of the cord
Scissors for the helper only
A tray with raised edges
steps: Before you start, the helper cuts the elastic cord to about 12 inches and ties a knot in one end.
Wrap a short piece of clear tape around the other end to make a stiff tip for threading.
Place the beads in the tray, inside the raised edges, and sit with the tray in front of you.
Take one bead at a time and slide it onto the taped end of the cord.
Keep going until the bracelet is long enough to go around the wrist, leaving a few inches free.
Hold the cord firmly and tie a knot at the free end, so no bead can slide off.
The helper trims the extra cord with the scissors.
Put the beads back in the tray, counting them as you go.
safety: Beads and small pieces are a choking hazard for children under three and for anyone who mouths things. Do not use beads with an under-three or with anyone who mouths objects.
Use large beads only after the person's safety has been considered. Keep loose beads in the tray, and count them out and back in.
Elastic cord can snap back. Tie the knot before you let go, and keep the cord away from the face and eyes.
Do not use resin or epoxy to hold or seal beads. The fumes and skin contact are a hazard.
Scissors are for the helper only.
An adult stays nearby while beads are in use, and a finished bracelet is never worn on the neck.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop with a few beads on the cord. Tie a knot, put the beads back in the tray and count them, and finish another day, or leave it as it is.

cards.name: Watch birds from a window
cards.summary: Sit by a window together, watch for birds, and describe their colors and how they move.
materials: A comfortable chair or bed positioned by a window with a view outside
A blanket or shawl for the lap
A sheet of paper and a few colored pencils or crayons
Binoculars or a magnifier, if they enjoy them
Optional: a bird feeder or bowl of water in view of the window
steps: Settle into a chair or bed by the window, with a blanket and a drink within reach.
Ask what they can see outside, or invite them to look for birds for a minute.
Wait quietly until a bird lands or flies past.
Ask what color the bird is, or what it is doing.
Trace the bird's path in the air with one finger, slowly, as it moves.
Draw a simple shape of the bird on the paper, using the color they name.
Listen for calls or song, and talk about how they sound.
Close the curtain if the glare is strong, and stop when they are ready.
safety: Window glare can be strong. Use a sheer curtain or move the chair so the sun is not in the eyes.
Glass can be cold in winter or hot in summer. Keep a blanket on the lap and the room at a comfortable temperature.
Keep the window closed or fitted with a safety stop. Never let anyone lean out to see a bird.
Check glasses are clean and on before watching, so details are easier to see.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop when the birds leave. Close the curtain, sit quietly together, and try again on another day.

cards.name: Weave paper strips
cards.summary: Weave colored paper strips over and under a card base that the helper has already slit.
materials: A sheet of thick card, about letter size, with parallel slits cut by the helper about one inch apart, stopping one inch short of the top and bottom edges
Colored paper or thin card in two or three colors, cut by the helper into strips about one inch wide
Scissors and a ruler for the helper
A glue stick or low-tack tape
steps: Lay the slit card on the table, with the slits running up and down and the strips within reach.
Choose the first strip together. Any color is fine.
Start at the bottom and push the strip over the first upright strip of card, then under the next, and so on across.
Pull the strip gently so it lies flat, but not so tight that the card bends.
For the next row, start the opposite way: under the first upright, then over the next.
Push each new row up against the last one, so the card is covered.
When a strip runs out, tape its end to the back of the card and start a new strip.
Stop when the card is covered, then tape down the loose ends on the back.
safety: Scissors are for the helper only. The person weaves with their hands alone.
Check the slit edges for sharp corners, and round them off with the helper before weaving.
Use a glue stick or low-tack tape, and keep small pieces away from the mouth.
cards.stopNote: It is fine to stop after one row. Leave the card on the table with the strips in place, and carry on another time, or just enjoy the colors.

cards.name: Wind a ball of yarn
cards.summary: Wind a skein or tangle of yarn into a neat ball together, taking turns holding and winding.
materials: A skein or loose length of soft, chunky yarn
A small bowl or basket for the finished ball
